title: HostedAPI KV cache leak amplification — post-incident notes and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

Severity: P0. 22-minute partial outage impacting hosted-api streaming sessions and ~8% elevated 5xx rate for gen endpoints in us-west-2 (2029-07-19 02:18–02:40 UTC). Customer-facing latency and tail errors for multi-turn chat workloads; some long-lived streaming sessions stalled requiring reconnects.

Impact:
- External: increased TTFB and intermittent 5xx for ~1.5% of overall requests in the region at peak; streaming chunk gaps caused client reconnects for high-concurrency customers.
- Internal: memory pressure and OOM restarts on a subset of worker pods due to unbounded KV cache growth on multiplexed nodes. Autoscaler reacted by adding nodes which briefly hid the scope.

High-level root cause hypothesis (summary):
A latent reference accounting bug in the runtime's KV-cache (multiplexer path) allowed certain prefix entries to remain pinned after session termination (leak). Under normal load the leak grows slowly. At 02:18 UTC an unrelated adaptive-batcher rollout increased batch window for a class of low-latency chat requests, which shifted request shapes and caused many more distinct prefixes to be cached. The cached population grew quickly; combined with the leak, per-node memory hit eviction thresholds and triggered aggressive eviction. Eviction path triggered repeated cache repopulation and contention on KV locks; that contention increased tail latency and led to streaming serialization stalls. Metric downsampling on the metric-aggregator masked the initial error signal until memory pressure caused OOM restarts and visible 5xx.

Timeline (timestamps UTC, best-effort assembled from telemetry and oncall notes):
- 02:10: config rollout: adaptive-batcher variant v2 rolled to 25% for us-west-2 (automated ramp).
- 02:17: subtle uptick in per-node resident size on multiplexers; not past alert thresholds.
- 02:18: client-facing latency SLO alert triggers (top-level latency alert). Oncall paged.
- 02:20: SRE looking at mem in dashboards sees cluster-level median mem rising; a small number of mux nodes show steady growth.
- 02:23: first OOM/restart observed on mux-147. Crash loops on a few mux nodes over next 3 minutes. 5xx rate climbs.
- 02:24: mitigation: rollback adaptive-batcher ramp to 0% (immediate reduction of new prefix patterns).
- 02:26: temporary mitigation: oncall set per-process cache soft limit via runtime flag and triggered graceful eviction for worst-affected hosts; began draining the two worst hosts.
- 02:32: stream stalls reduced as eviction completed and restarted pods came up with bounded memory. 5xx rate returning to baseline.
- 02:40: incident declared resolved; monitoring in recovery mode and SRE remain on pager for 4 hours.

Detection and gaps in monitoring: 
- The metric-aggregator compressed some high-cardinality per-prefix metrics; our alerting used a downsampled memory trend and missed the early growth (alert only after OOM).
- KV mutex contention and queueing were not surfaced by any single dashboard; we relied on ad-hoc traces.

Immediate mitigations taken: 
1) Roll back adaptive-batcher change (02:24) — stopped new request shapes that drove cache population.
2) Apply per-process cache soft limit flag on mux nodes (02:26) to avoid OOM and allow graceful eviction.
3) Drain and recycle the worst-affected mux nodes in controlled canary batches (02:27–02:32).
4) Short-term lock: enable a runtime path that bypasses KV-prefetch for streaming sessions for customers in the impacted routing tier (02:28) — quick binary toggle.

Root cause analysis (detailed):
- Bug: reference accounting in the KV cache had a path where certain prefix entries allocated during prefix-merge were not decremented on session teardown when a multiplexed session took a fast failure path. This left entries effectively pinned.
- Amplifier: adaptive-batcher rollout increased the variety of prefixes being cached per unit time (more distinct token-prefix combos). The leak that previously held steady became exponential relative to new prefix arrival rate.
- Contention feedback loop: eviction caused heavy lock thrashing and repopulation; repeated repopulation caused more allocations and lock contention, which increased request tail times, causing more sessions to enter failure paths, producing more pinned entries.
- Observability shortfall: downsampled telemetry and an alert threshold tied to cluster median memory hid the per-host signal. No alert existed for sustained per-pod resident growth on mux processes.

Post-incident remediation plan (short + medium + long):
Short (done or in-progress):
- Hotfix PR merged that adds reference decrement on the failure path (PR linked). Deploy to canary then region. (Owner: Marco Ruiz, due 2029-07-20 — PR 5821)
- Add an emergency runtime flag to cap per-process cache memory; make flag default-safe (Owner: Lina Chen, done)
- Update oncall checklist with immediate steps to throttle adaptive-batcher and to toggle KV-prefetch bypass (Owner: Devon Brooks, done)

Medium (1–3 weeks):
- Add per-pod resident memory alerts for mux processes (SLO/alerting change). Create burn-in test with high unique-prefix load to exercise cache growth. (Owner: eng-sre, due 2029-07-30)
- Add a high-cardinality telemetry path for prefix churn (sampled but sufficient to detect growth pattern). (Owner: Observability team, due 2029-07-25)
- Add lock contention metrics / histograms exposed from runtime to the standard mux dashboard. (Owner: serving-runtime team, due 2029-07-26)

Long (quarter):
- Rework eviction policy to prefer TTL+usage heuristics and avoid repopulation oscillation; evaluate adaptive eviction backoff. (Owner: serving-runtime, due 2029-09-30)
- Introduce chaos/scale tests simulating adaptive-batcher rollouts and high unique-prefix arrival to ensure the runtime behaves under exponentiating prefix sets. (Owner: SRE + QE, due 2029-10-15)

Runbook draft for oncall (new steps to insert into Hosted API runbook):
- Initial triage: check hosted-api top-line latency and 5xx dashboards, then jump to mux process mem-resident chart (per-pod).
- If per-pod resident growth > 80% of expected cap for 3 consecutive minutes:
  a) Toggle runtime flag 'kv-prefetch-bypass' on routing tier to stop prefetch.
  b) Set per-process soft cache limit (runtime flag) to 60% and trigger graceful eviction.
  c) If nodes show OOMs: drain the worst affected pods and restart, keeping concurrency low.
- If lock contention visible (high syscall wait + mutex hist): reduce adaptive-batcher window or rollback recent batcher rollout.
- Escalation: if 5xx > 3% region-wide and persists > 10 minutes, page eng-sre lead and serving-runtime oncall.

Action items (owners + due dates):
- SRE-3472: Add per-pod resident alerts and sampling for prefix churn. (Owner: Lina Chen, due 2029-07-25)
- Fix PR 5821: reference accounting bug patch and unit tests. (Owner: Marco Ruiz, merged; monitor canary 24h)
- Dashboard: mux contention and mem growth view and playbook links. (Owner: Observability, due 2029-07-23)
- Runbook: formalize steps above and publish to Confluence (Owner: Devon Brooks, due 2029-07-22)

Open questions / follow-ups: 
- Are there other fast-fail code paths that can create pinned prefixes? Need a code audit across mux fast paths. (Owner: Serving-runtime)
- Can the adaptive-batcher logic be more conservative about introducing new prefix shapes during ramp? (Product + Serving Runtime)
- Verify whether autoscaler behavior can be tuned so memory-driven scaling adds nodes earlier to avoid OOM cascades, or whether soft-limits are safer as primary defense.

Notes on communication:
- Incident timeline and customer-facing summary prepared for CS (short blurb) and Legal (impact summary).
- No customer data was exposed. Root cause was purely runtime resource management.

Appendix: artifacts used to construct this doc:
- Heap snapshots and resident memory time series from mux nodes (archived to S3, link in JIRA).
- Flame graphs showing lock contention (attached to PR).
- Correlated request traces across prefix churn window (sampling 1%).

Postmortem status: draft — pending review from serving-runtime and product (batching owners). Once the hotfix proves stable in canary for 24h and alerts are added, mark final and close SRE-3472.

If you were oncall and want to reproduce locally: start the mux with the provided stress harness (repo/serving-runtime/tools/mux-stress), set unique-prefix rate to 10k/min and enable the failure-path toggles. This reproduces the leak within ~30 minutes today.

Contact for follow-ups: Aisha Patel (owner), Marco Ruiz (hotfix PR), Lina Chen (alerts/dashboards), Devon Brooks (runbook update).
